name: Mikhail Tal
tagline: The Magician Who Played Through Pain
story:
In 1959, a 23-year-old from Riga sat across the board from Mikhail Botvinnik, the reigning World Chess Champion and a man who had dominated the game for over a decade. Mikhail Tal was already missing a kidney — removed due to chronic illness — and doctors had warned him that the physical toll of a world championship match could be devastating. He played anyway.

Tal's style was unlike anything chess had seen. Where others calculated with cold precision, he conjured chaos. He sacrificed pieces with an almost reckless abandon, creating positions so bewilderingly complex that even grandmasters couldn't see through them. Botvinnik, the great scientist of chess, found himself drowning in complications he couldn't untangle. Tal won the match and became the youngest World Chess Champion in history at that time.

But the real grit came after. Tal lost the rematch a year later. His kidney problems worsened. He spent months in hospitals, enduring surgery after surgery — over a dozen operations throughout his life. Each time, he returned to the board. Between hospital stays, he won tournament after tournament, played some of the most beautiful games in chess history, and maintained a record-setting 95-game unbeaten streak. He played blitz chess in hospital corridors with his IV still attached.

Tal died at 55, his body ravaged by decades of illness. But he never played a cautious game in his life. When asked why he sacrificed pieces in positions where he couldn't calculate all the variations, he said simply: 'You see, I was just sure.' Some people play it safe when the odds are against them. Tal set the board on fire and dared the universe to stop him.
